The point of riposte

Source: POINT.md

riposte is an R package for researchers who analyze randomized experiments — completely randomized, block-randomized, or cluster-randomized — and want to test the sharp null hypothesis that treatment changed no one’s outcome. A difference of means can miss an effect that changes the spread of the outcomes or changes the outcomes of only a few units. riposte combines several representations of the outcome (raw values, ranks, distances, a bounded transform) into one test with power against such effects. It compares the observed test statistic with its distribution over re-randomizations of treatment, so the chance of rejecting a true sharp null hypothesis is at most the level the researcher chose, in samples of any size. When a user picks a large-sample approximation instead, the printed result says that it is an approximation.

For matched pairs, riposte also offers Rosenbaum’s sensitivity analysis for observational studies. The researcher chooses gamma: an unmeasured difference between the two units of a pair could have made one unit’s odds of treatment as much as gamma times the other’s. riposte reports an upper bound on the p-value, the largest p-value that hidden bias no larger than gamma could produce. At gamma = 1 that bound is the p-value of a paired randomized experiment. Under the sharp null hypothesis only the signs of the treated-minus-control differences depend on which unit was treated, so riposte computes the bound from the chance of each pattern of signs, by listing every pattern or by drawing patterns at random. It uses a normal approximation only when the user asks for one.

The package is the software for Bowers and Burton, “A More Powerful Test for Randomized Experiments”: a reader of the paper can run its tests on their own experiment.

riposte tests hypotheses. It does not estimate the size of effects (propertee), locate effects among blocks (manytestsr), or count the units harmed (CMRSS).

Developed by Jake Bowers, Myla Burton.
